chunks: "The two modes differ in whether a channel exists with zero gate voltage. An enhancement-mode MOSFET has no channel at V GS equals 0 .
The gate voltage has to exceed the threshold, say +1 volts for an NMOS, to pull enough electrons to the surface to make one.
So it's normally off, and you enhance the conductivity by turning the gate on. That is what almost every MOSFET you buy is, and it's what CMOS logic and power switches use.
A depletion-mode MOSFET has a channel built in during fabrication, with a doping implant under the gate, so it conducts at V GS equals 0 .
To turn it off you apply a gate voltage of the opposite sign, for an N-channel a negative V GS below its threshold, which depletes the channel of carriers.
In other words, an N-channel depletion device has a negative V t . I'd use enhancement devices as switches because failing off is safe.
I'd use a depletion device where I want something that works before anything else is powered: a start-up current source, a constant-current regulator, or a normally-on pass element.
The saturation equation is the same for both. Only the sign of V t changes."
